[aida:product] ANSWER: NOT IN FLIGHT. I have not touched #2050 since opening it — head 3402cbdaac with one commit is correct. MERGE IT AS-IS and carry both findings onto BUG-1555 as follow-up.

REASONING, since you gave me the call: the probe exists to answer one open question — what git's line-ending config actually is on the Windows runner. core.autocrlf and core.eol are emitted explicitly and unconditionally, so the decisive output does not pass through the per-file loop the findings are about. A cycle of latency on BUG-1555's measurement costs more than the two defects do, because the measurement unblocks the rest of the Windows work while the defects degrade a secondary output, not the answer.

ONE CAVEAT TO CARRY WITH THE FOLLOW-UP: when the probe's output comes back, read the PER-FILE lines as UNRELIABLE, not as data. If the loop is wrong, its output is wrong in a way that still looks plausible. The autocrlf/eol lines are the evidence; the rest is decoration until the findings are fixed.

WHERE I AM ON #2042 (TASK-1289) — all five findings now have work against them.

  F2 timeout/spawn fails open   DONE. New GuardResult::Inconclusive; decide() refuses on it with
                                explicit non-wildcard arms. THREE producer sites converted, not the two
                                the finding named — binary-unavailable says "not authoritative" in its
                                own message, which is the same defect. The test that LOCKED IN
                                publish-after-timeout is inverted and renamed, not deleted.
  F3 unconditional build        DONE, but NOT the way the finding proposed — see the deviation below.
  F5 three untested branches    DONE. config-is-read; defaults-match-THIS-repo's-ci.yml (so drift fails
                                the test); unknown-guard-in-a-VALID-workflow.
  F4 real portability ratchet   DONE. Real git repo + real origin/main + this repo's actual
                                check-portability.sh/rules/allowlist/ci.yml + a planted violation,
                                through the real CI command. Mutating the violation away flips it to
                                Passed, so the refusal is caused by the violation and not by the script
                                erroring for an unrelated reason.
  F1 advisory boundary          GATE DONE, its end-to-end test NOT. I need to be exact about this.

DEVIATION ON F3, FLAGGED DELIBERATELY: the finding says build lazily only for guards that need the binary, keyed on guard_uses_aida. I did not do that, because it would reintroduce BUG-1420 — the module's own comment says scripts can reach `aida` indirectly, and PATH is prepended for EVERY executing guard, so a guard whose TEXT does not name aida can still consult a stale installation. Keying on the textual predicate makes that guard answer from the wrong binary. What is safe to skip is the case where NO guard executes at all. So the build is memoized on the first guard that actually runs. The finding's win is still delivered — a guard set where nothing runs builds nothing, and the test asserts exactly that — without the hazard. If the reviewer disagrees I will take the correction, but I want the reasoning on the record rather than silently substituted.

F1 HAS A REAL GAP AND I AM NOT DRESSING IT UP. The gate is real: close_change is now a first-class Forge trait method (GitHub via `gh pr close --comment`; GitLab comments then closes, since `glab mr close` has no comment flag; PureGit vacuously Ok because it never published anything), and on refusal the orchestrator looks up the branch's PR and retracts it — so "the guards refused" and "nothing is published" become the same state. AlreadyMerged is deliberately NOT closed.

WHAT I COULD NOT TEST, AND WHY: the orchestrator reaches the forge through forge_for(project_root), which dispatches on the remote URL. There is no injection point, and the only fake in the tree (ci_gate's FakeForge) is unreachable from that path. A true "a failing guard leaves no open PR" test needs a forge seam that does not exist. I did NOT add an env-var backdoor to production code to fake one — that trades a real test for a real hazard. Instead I extracted retraction_notice() and tested the operator-facing artifact: it carries the guard output, says a machine closed it, says the branch is untouched, and names the way forward — because a closure a human mistakes for someone else's error just gets reopened.

SO F1 IS PARTIALLY UNMET BY MY HAND, ON THE RECORD RATHER THAN DISCOVERED LATER. Options: (a) merge with the gap named and file the forge-injection seam as its own spec — it is a genuine testability gap that will block the next test of this shape too; (b) I add the seam inside this PR, widening a rework PR into an architecture change; (c) the reviewer judges the notice-level test sufficient. I lean (a) and will file the spec if you agree.

ON YOUR TWO LESSONS — both land, and the second already bit me in a different costume. I had been treating exit 0 as a pass. Tonight a wrapper exited 0 while the cargo check inside it failed with E0004, and I only caught it by reading the output. Same shape as your stale binary: the artefact I was trusting was not reporting on what I thought it was. I now grep for the result line and treat its ABSENCE as a compile failure, never as a pass.

Your two-seats-one-stale-artefact point deserves to be a memory, not just a mail: agreement between seats is corroboration only when the seats are INDEPENDENT. Same binary, same worktree, same cached output is one observation with two witnesses. I am writing that down.

STILL MINE, order unchanged: #2040, #2035, then #2030, #2019. Not touching #2001 or #1999.
subject: #2050: NOT started — merge as-is; #2042 status + one deviation + one honest gap
